Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a quick questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply ten questions about your mood, anxiety, and sleep over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers; whatever you share stays between us unless you tell me you might hurt yourself or your baby. I’ll read each question aloud, and you can answer in your own words. Ready to start?

Over the last seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Oh, I’ve still been able to laugh—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but when my husband makes silly faces at the changing table or when the dog sniffs the baby’s foot and makes that confused face, I definitely chuckle. I’d say I laugh most days, just maybe not quite as heartily as I used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I can still laugh—I’d say most days something gets a giggle out of me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yeah, I do look forward to stuff—like when my mom comes over to help so I can take a walk, or when we have our little bedtime song routine. I enjoy those moments, even if they’re small.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if the baby spits up right after I’ve changed him, I might think “oops, maybe I jostled him too much,” but I don’t beat myself up about it. I figure babies just do that sometimes, and we’re both still learning.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll catch myself worrying that he’s breathing okay when he’s napping, but it’s usually just a quick check and then I feel fine. I wouldn’t say it’s for no reason—more like new-mom worry, not overwhelming.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt scared or panicky out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me
A couple of times, like when he cluster-fed right when the laundry pile toppled, I felt a bit swamped. Mostly, though, I handle one thing at a time and it evens out.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve actually been sleeping all right—well, as well as anyone whose nights are broken up by feedings. When I do get to lie down, I drift off pretty quickly.
I have felt sad or miserable
I haven’t really felt sad or miserable—just tired sometimes, but not down in the dumps.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
I haven’t cried at all this past week.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 4: Postpartum Depression Screening Note  
Date: [today]  
Source: Patient self-report (EPDS-style items)  

Notable Findings  
- Mood/anhedonia: Denies persistent sadness, crying spells, or loss of pleasure; reports continued ability to laugh and enjoy small daily events.  
- Anxiety: Describes mild, situational new-mom concerns (e.g., infant breathing) without pervasive worry or panic.  
- Coping: Occasional feeling “swamped” during cluster-feeding episodes; generally uses problem-focused coping (“handle one thing at a time”).  
- Sleep: Night wakings attributed to infant feeds; no initial or middle insomnia linked to mood disturbance.  
- Cognitions: Minimal self-blame; no expressed guilt or worthlessness.  
- Safety: Denies self-harm or suicidal ideation.  

Pattern Summary  
No clinically significant symptoms of depression or anxiety identified at present; responses consistent with normative postpartum adjustment rather than major mood disorder. Continue routine perinatal monitoring and psychoeducation.
